case_name: Burrell v. Regional Municipality of Peel Police Services Board
text:
COURT
FILE NO.:
01-CV-211652

SUPERIOR COURT OF
JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
EMLIN
BURRELL v. THE REGIONAL MUNICIPALITY OF PEEL POLICE SERVICES BOARD, CHIEF OF
POLICE NOEL CATNEY, POLICE SERGEANT CONROY, POLICE CONSTABLE K. GRAHAM and
POLICE CONSTABLE R. KETT

BEFORE:
Master
R. Dash

COUNSEL:
Ernest Guiste, for the
plaintiff

Maria Kotsopoulos, for the
defendants

COSTS ENDORSEMENT

[
1
]

On September 25, 2007 I heard the defendant’s
motion to dismiss or stay the action for non-payment of two costs orders. By
endorsement released November 2, 2007 I ordered that the action be stayed until
the first of two costs orders were paid. This endorsement deals with the costs
of the motion to dismiss as well as the costs of the plaintiff’s cross-motion
to vary the costs orders, which motion was dismissed by me on July 23, 2007.

[
2
]

I ordered the action stayed until the October
19, 2006 costs award was paid despite the plaintiff’s impecuniosity, because
the award arose out of the plaintiff’s cavalier attitude to orders of the court
and to her total abandonment of her obligations as a litigant. I noted that her
solicitor had failed to make any attempt to answer or even look at outstanding
undertakings or to comply with a court order to which he had consented.
Although the award was made against the plaintiff, and not her solicitor, I
made it clear that the solicitor’s failure to give the file any attention
whatsoever led to the costs award and I invited him to pay the costs for which
he was clearly responsible.
[1]

If the stay was lifted by payment of the costs within six months I would allow
the action to proceed notwithstanding non-payment of the December 18, 2006
costs award, since although those costs were properly awarded against the
plaintiff, they did not result from the same sort of egregious conduct as
resulted in the first award.

ENTITLEMENT TO COSTS

[
3
]

The difficulty now is the award of costs for
this motion to dismiss. The defendants had incurred significant costs in
compelling the plaintiff to comply with her court-ordered obligations which
resulted in the first costs order, and have now incurred additional costs in
enforcing payment of those costs. The plaintiff resisted this motion to dismiss
or stay the action and in the course thereof has forced five attendances on that
motion and brought three intervening motions to vary the costs orders, one of
which was withdrawn and two of which were unsuccessful. The defendants were
successful in defeating the last motion to vary before me and in obtaining a
stay of the action, both of which motions are the subject matter of this costs
endorsement.
[2]

[
4
]

The defendant suggests there was “clear divided
success” on the motions. I disagree. Although the action was stayed pending
payment of costs, and not dismissed, a stay was the alternate relief claimed by
the defendants and the plaintiff opposed both a dismissal and a stay. Although
the action was stayed pending payment of only one of two costs awards, that
order required a significant indulgence by the court to the plaintiff and
cannot be considered a success. The plaintiff was unsuccessful on the motion to
vary. The defendants acted reasonably throughout and as will be seen, the
plaintiff caused unnecessary costs to be incurred. There is no question in my
mind that the defendants were substantially successful on both motions and are
entitled to their costs. The issues are quantum, who should pay the costs (the
plaintiff or her solicitor) and the timing of payment. The plaintiff’s
impecuniosity is raised as a factor in this determination.

[
5
]

Costs are a matter within the discretion of the
judge or master hearing a motion and the court may determine by whom and to
what extent costs shall be paid.
[3]

The court is to take into account the factors listed in rule 57.01 and make a
costs award that is fair and reasonable in the circumstances. In accordance
with rule 57.03(1) the presumptive rule is that costs are fixed by the motions
judge or master and payable within 30 days, although a different order may be
made if more just.

[
6
]

The defendants’ motion was first returnable on
January 29, 2007 before Master Brott. Prior to the return of the motion the
plaintiff served a motion to vary my orders. Both motions were adjourned to me.
On March 8 both motions were before me and could have been heard, however Mr.
Guiste withdrew the motion to vary and at his request the motion to dismiss was
adjourned so that he could bring the motion to vary before a judge, despite
suggestions both from myself and from defendants’ counsel that it would be more
appropriate to have any motion to vary my orders heard by me. Brown J.
dismissed the motion to vary on April 30, 2007 because it was more properly an
appeal and there were no grounds to vary under rule 59.06.
[4]
The motion to dismiss next came
before me on June 7, but was again adjourned because Mr. Guiste was booked in
another courtroom. By the time the matter came back before me on July 23 Mr.
Guiste had served yet another motion to vary, this time before me. That motion
was argued and dismissed on similar grounds to that articulated by Brown J.,
but the scheduled time ran out before I could hear the defendants’ motion to
dismiss. Finally on September 25 the defendants’ motion to dismiss or stay was
heard on its merits.

[
7
]

Throughout, the defendants were
forced to continue to incur substantial expense while Mr. Guiste sought
adjournment after adjournment and brought not one, not two, but three motions
to vary, one withdrawn and two heard.
There is a
reasonable expectation that the defaulting plaintiff will bear at least a
portion of those costs.

COSTS PERSONALLY AGAINST THE SOLICITOR

[
8
]

The defendants argue that the costs be payable
by Mr. Guiste personally under rule 57.07. Rules 57.07(1) and (2) provide:

57.07
(1)
Where a solicitor for
a party has caused costs to be incurred without reasonable cause or to be
wasted by undue delay, negligence or other default, the court may make an
order,

(a) disallowing costs between the solicitor and client or directing the
solicitor to repay to the client money paid on account of costs;

(b) directing the solicitor to reimburse the client for any costs that
the client has been ordered to pay to any other party; and

(c) requiring the solicitor personally to pay the costs of any party.

(2)
An order under subrule (1) may be
made by the court on its own initiative or on the motion of any party to the
proceeding, but no such order shall be made unless the solicitor is given a
reasonable opportunity to make representations to the court.

The defendants provided the notice
required under rule 57.01(2) and Mr. Guiste has made submissions on the merits
of such order.

[
9
]

The defendants submit that Mr. Guiste pay the
costs personally because of his decision to argue the motion to vary on at
least three separate occasions, because impecuniosity had already been rejected
on the original motion when the costs order was made, because several warnings
had been given that a motion to vary was ill-founded and because of his
“general tactic of delay.” They suggest that Mr. Guiste pursued a strategy that
was not only unattainable, but was designed to delay the hearing of the
defendants’ motion to dismiss with no rational basis and to cause the
defendants to incur excessive costs responding to each new tactical manoeuvre
and motion.

[
10
]

Mr. Guiste argues that as an advocate he must be creative and
fearless and that the steps he took were to safeguard the best interests of his
client given “her limited resources and the vital importance of her case.” As a
general proposition this is undoubtedly true, but it is not without limits – in
taking such steps he must not cause “costs to be
incurred without reasonable cause or to be wasted by undue delay, negligence or
other default”. He denies taking steps with the
intention of making the litigation more expensive. While this denial rings
somewhat hollow, it is not necessary that I determine his intention – what is
relevant are his actions.

[
11
]

In the recent decision of
Walsh v. 1124660 Ontario Limited
[5]
, Lane J. had to determine
whether to award costs personally against Mr. Guiste following a lengthy jury
trial. Lane J. extensively reviewed the law with respect to costs personally
against a solicitor, and its development since the Supreme Court of Canada
decision in
Young v. Young
[6]

and the subsequent passage of rule 57.07. I would summarize the law from that
decision as follows:

1.

It is no longer necessary to show abuse of
process, contempt of court, bad faith or gross negligence to award costs
personally against a solicitor. Rule 57.07 has enlarged the ambit of such
orders to include costs incurred “without reasonable
cause or to be wasted by undue delay, negligence or other default”. It “is enough that the acts described in the Rule have occurred”.

[7]

2.

Courts however must be “extremely cautious” in
making such awards given the duties of a lawyer to guard confidentiality of
instructions and to “bring forward a client’s case with courage”, to represent
a client “resolutely and honourably within the limits of the law”, to “raise
fearlessly every issue [and] advance every argument” that would assist his
client’s case, to “bring forward with courage even unpopular causes”, and to
“accept and argue cases without fear of costs orders against him should the
case turn out to be a weak one”.
[8]

[
12
]

Lane J. summarizes how these two principles work together in the
following passage:

Another duty of counsel is to promote the
client's case through fearless advocacy and the marshalling of all the evidence
which may reasonably support that case. Here again, it would be subversive of
the proper role of counsel for the court to "second-guess" the way in
which this duty was performed, simply because the court thinks in hindsight
that it might have been done better or differently or more wisely or less
abrasively or more economically as to time. It is only where expense has been
incurred
without reasonable cause,
or there has
been waste of costs through
undue
delay,
negligence or other
default
, that the court can
intervene. It seems to me that the reasonableness of the expense is to be judged
as at the time it was incurred, or foisted on the opposite party, and not with
the benefit of hindsight.
[9]

[emphasis in original
decision of Lane J.]

[
13
]

The defendants have incurred actual costs of $28,897 although they
claim costs on a partial indemnity basis in the amount of $22,806. These
include the costs of the attendance before Master Brott on January 29 and the
four appearances before me on March 8, June 7, July 23 and September 25, but
not the appearance before Brown J. on April 27, 2007 as those costs were dealt
with by Brown J. I will deal with the issue of quantum later in this
endorsement, but suffice it to say that the costs were dramatically increased
because of the actions of the plaintiff’s counsel bringing on a motion to vary
in response to the motion to dismiss, withdrawing the motion to vary in favour
of a motion to vary before a judge, bringing on a further motion to vary before
me after the same relief was denied by a judge and then finally dealing with
the defendants’ motion to dismiss on its merits.

[
14
]

Were the actions of plaintiff’s counsel on this motion reasonable?
Did the actions taken by plaintiff’s counsel go beyond fearless advocacy and
cause expense to be incurred without reasonable cause or wasted through
unreasonable delay, negligence or other default?

[
15
]

I accept that Mr. Guiste had a right, if not a duty, to take
reasonable steps to avoid dismissal of the plaintiff’s action resulting from
costs orders she could not pay. The means by which he did this was not
reasonable. The proper procedure would have been to move for leave to appeal
the original costs orders, which he did not do. That being the case, the
reasonable step would have been to attend upon the defendant’s motion to
dismiss on its original return date of January 29 and argue that a dismissal
would not be just – the argument that was ultimately made on September 25,
2007, the sixth court date concerned with enforcing my costs awards. Both Brown
J. and I found the motion to vary ill-founded, but if such motion were to be
argued it should have been heard on the second court appearance on March 8,
2007, together with the defendants’ motion to dismiss. Once the motion to vary
before me was withdrawn and then heard and dismissed by a judge, it should never
have been brought back on before me for what was then the third such motion. As
a result the defendants’ motion to dismiss, which could have been heard on the
first or second court appearance, was not heard until the fifth appearance
before the Master and after an appearance before Brown J.

[
16
]

In his defence Mr. Guiste says that after the costs ruling he
attempted to do the reasonable thing and negotiate terms for payment. I dealt
with that argument in paragraph 62 of my reasons for decision on this motion.
No concrete proposal was ever made.

[
17
]

In my view, Mr. Guiste has caused costs to be incurred without
reasonable cause and through undue delay, negligence or other default. This is
not a matter of the court second-guessing the actions of Mr. Guiste or in
hindsight concluding that the steps taken by him could have been done
differently or more economically. I say this because it was made clear to Mr.
Guiste in advance that the plaintiff’s motion to vary and the defendants’
motion to dismiss should be heard together by me since I was the judicial
officer who made the original costs order which the defendants were attempting
to enforce and the plaintiff was seeking to vary. He was also told several
times that the motion to vary was ill-founded. As early as the first attendance
on January 29, 2007 Master Brott stated that both motions should be heard
together and they should be heard by me. Then on the first appearance before me
on March 8, when Mr. Guiste withdrew the motion to vary in favour of a new
motion to vary before a judge, I noted in my endorsement on that date that “the
motion to vary should be heard by me as I made the original orders” although I
noted his right to move before a judge. I also suggested to Mr. Guiste that his
motion to vary may be ill-conceived because “the plaintiff failed to appeal my
orders” and because “the grounds raised to vary appear not to fall within rule
59.06.”  These were exactly the grounds upon which Brown J. dismissed the
motion to vary. He stated that the plaintiff was arguing that my costs orders
were wrong in law and that an appeal was the proper route to follow. He noted
that the plaintiff had decided not to appeal, that on the motion to vary she
was in effect seeking to appeal, but that there were no grounds to vary under
rule 59.06 as there was no slip or omission or change in circumstances. Having
lost the motion to vary before Brown J., the motion to dismiss was scheduled to
be heard by me on June 7. The motion was again adjourned because Mr. Guiste was
double booked. Before the next appearance on July 23 Mr. Guiste served a fresh
motion to vary returnable before me, on similar grounds as he had raised on the
first motion to vary before me, which he withdrew on March 8 and which he
argued unsuccessfully before Brown J. on April 27. On July 23 I dismissed the
motion to vary on essentially the same basis as stated by Brown J. These were
the same grounds upon which Mr. Guiste had been warned on March 8, 2007.

[
18
]

I also note that the thrust of Mr. Guiste’s submissions on both
motions to vary and on the motion to dismiss was that his client was
impecunious and would be denied access to justice if forced to pay the costs
awarded on October 19, 2006 and on December 18, 2006. He suggested that
knowledge of the actual amount of income and expenses demonstrating the
plaintiff’s impecuniosity was new evidence not available before me on in
October 2006. I had however already accepted and taken into account his
client’s impecuniosity on the hearing of the original dismissal motion which
resulted in the order of October 19, 2006 to pay costs.

[
19
]

The court is therefore not second guessing Mr. Guiste or suggesting
a better route to take in hindsight. It is just the opposite. Mr. Guiste was
advised early in the process that the motions should be heard by me, that the
proper route to follow was an appeal and that there were no grounds to vary
under rule 59.06, yet he moved for the relief before Brown J. and after Brown
J. dismissed the motion, he moved yet again before me. Mr. Guiste should be
responsible at least for that portion of the plaintiff’s costs incurred as a
result of his unreasonable actions, and in particular the appearances on March
8, June 7 and July 23 and any costs thrown away for repeated preparation.

[
20
]

I have reviewed the defendants’ dockets and considered the expenses
that the defendants have been forced to incur as a result of Mr. Guiste’s
unreasonable actions. While the percentage may be significantly greater, in my
view it is fair and reasonable that Mr. Guiste be personally responsible for at
least one third of the defendants’ costs.

COSTS AGAINST THE IMPECUNIOUS PLAINTIFF

[
21
]

The question then remains whether the plaintiff should be personally
responsible for the balance of the costs and if so when they should be paid.
Mr. Guiste argues that no costs be awarded against his client because the
defendant is a state actor “and the plaintiff is a poor citizen.” Although not
explicitly stated in his costs submissions, I consider the arguments Mr. Guiste
made on the substantive motion, namely that his client is impecunious, cannot
pay the costs of this motion and that if ordered to do so, she will be denied
access to the courts, and in the alternative, costs should be payable after
trial by way of set off against any costs or damages awarded to the plaintiff.

[
22
]

I set out in great detail in my November 2, 2007 reasons
[10]
the law as it relates to
impecuniosity as a factor in the award of costs and I need not repeat it in
this endorsement. It is a relevant factor to consider, but it is a matter of
the court’s discretion to what extent, if any, it should be taken into account
in the award of costs. The court must be mindful about foreclosing the
plaintiff’s access to justice if an award of costs is made that she cannot pay
as well as the rights of the defendants who have incurred substantial costs in
compelling the plaintiff to comply with her obligations as a litigant. While a person has a right of access to the courts she must accept
the accompanying responsibility to comply with its rules and orders. The plaintiff cannot ignore the rules and orders of the court and
then use impecuniosity as a shield against the costs consequences of her
actions. There must be fairness and a balancing of interests, but clearly a
person’s modest means cannot serve as an excuse to play by a different set of
procedural rules.

[
23
]

As Perell J. stated in
Christian Jew Foundation
, the court
should “probe the circumstances and assess…the procedural good faith of the
party using impecuniosity as his or her excuse for failing to comply with a
court order” and suggested the court ask: “
Is the person using impecuniosity as a means to avoid his
or her responsibilities or in good faith as an apology or explanation for
failing to do so?”
[11]

In my reasons on the motion to dismiss, I determined
that there had been no reasonable excuse for the plaintiff’s actions and that
she was using her impecuniosity as a means to avoid responsibilities for her
actions.

[
24
]

The plaintiff personally attended every court appearance before me
on this motion. I do not recall if she was present when the costs orders were
made in 2006, but given her attendances on the current motion to dismiss or
stay her action for failure to comply with the orders, she was clearly aware of
the existence of the costs awards made against her and the reasons why they
were made. She was also aware of the various adjournment requests and motions
brought by Mr. Guiste on her behalf to vary the orders. As I indicated in my
reasons on the current motion to dismiss, I accepted that as an impecunious
litigant, the plaintiff would be unable to pay the costs of the October 19,
2006 order herself within six months as ordered and that if the stay were to be
lifted and a dismissal avoided, Mr. Guiste would have to step up to the plate
and personally pay the costs for which he was clearly responsible.
[12]

[
25
]

The plaintiff was aware of the steps taken by her solicitor on these
motions. As a result of the 2006 costs orders she was aware that costs may be
awarded against a losing party to a motion, including a person in her financial
circumstances. In my view she should not now be permitted to hide behind a
shield of impecuniosity to avoid responsibility for the costs incurred with her
knowledge and apparent consent in these current motions.
[13]
If I simply allowed the
plaintiff to pay all of these costs after trial and set them off against
damages which might be awarded to her, it would allow her to continue with
unreasonable procedures and cause the defendants to incur needless costs with
no consequences other than a possible set-off at the end of the day IF she wins
at trial. Of course, if she loses at trial the defendants will never collect
these or any other costs in the action and her behaviour would remain forever
unsanctioned.

[
26
]

There is a reasonable expectation that an impecunious plaintiff who
embarks upon a path of numerous unsuccessful motions will bear at least a
portion of those costs. As Brown J. stated on June 8,
2007 in considering the costs of the motion before him to vary my costs orders:

If, having brought a claim, a party of modest means
proceeds to embark upon a procedural path that involves numerous unsuccessful
interlocutory motions, or seeks procedural relief from the justice system, but
then fails to comply with orders made by judicial officers, fairness dictates
that the other party should receive some compensation for the legal expense to
which it has been put, notwithstanding the limited resources of the other
party.  A person’s modest financial position cannot serve as an excuse to
play by a different set of procedural rules.
[14]

[
27
]

I cannot however ignore her financial condition. Her evidence of
income (from disability pensions) and expenses indicates an excess of $102.70
per month. Although she has not provided the court with her tax returns that
may indicate other income, such as provincial tax credits, I am prepared to
accept her stated income for purposes of this motion. Part of her monthly
recurring expenses is a $25 charitable donation. While charitable giving is a
worthwhile activity to be encouraged among Canadians of all income brackets, it
may not be an expense the plaintiff can afford at this time while she is in
litigation and unreasonably bringing and resisting motions that result in the
defendants incurring significant costs. In my view the plaintiff can afford,
perhaps with some difficulty, payments of $50 per month toward the costs award.
The balance will be payable after trial. Those payments should be sufficient to
bring home to the plaintiff that there is a price to pay for unreasonable
behaviour. Of course the costs payable by the plaintiff will be reduced by the
award made personally against Mr. Guiste.

QUANTUM OF COSTS

[
28
]

With respect to quantum, Mr. Guiste in his submissions indicated
that he would like to cross-examine the defendants on their Costs Outline
because “they are simply not reasonable.” He provided what he referred to as
his preliminary submissions reserving further submissions until after
cross-examination. There is no authority for cross-examination on costs
submissions or on a Costs Outline. Mr. Guiste was provided with the defendants’
detailed dockets in addition to the Costs Outline and submissions. Since costs
are not a simple exercise of multiplying hours by an hourly rate, Mr. Guiste
could have provided his submissions at this time as to the quantum of costs
that would be fair and reasonable in the circumstances. Notwithstanding that
opportunity, Mr. Guiste restricted his submissions to argument that no costs
should be payable by him and that no costs should be payable by his client,
while ignoring the issue of quantum except the bald assertion that they were
not reasonable. I intend to fix costs based on the material and submissions
currently before me.

[
29
]

I have considered the factors set out in rule 57.07(1) in order to
determine an award of costs that would be fair and reasonable in the
circumstances.

[
30
]

As indicated, although there was some division of success, the
defendants obtained the alternate relief sought, namely a stay of the action. I
was not advised of any specific offers to settle the motion. The plaintiff
seeks over $1 million and has made serious allegations of Charter violations.
The motions were very important to both parties, as the right to continue with
the action was at stake. The issues were further important to the defendants
because from their perspective the plaintiff was using her impecuniosity to
shield her from substantial costs she was causing them to incur and to the
plaintiff because from her perspective the motions affected her access to
justice. The legal and factual issues on the motion were somewhat complex as
the role of impecuniosity and access to justice on a motion to dismiss for
failure to pay a costs award needed to be examined, as did the rights of a
party to seek a variation on the grounds argued by the plaintiff.

[
31
]

The conduct of the plaintiff and her solicitor lengthened the
duration of these motions and significantly increased the costs of the
defendants by bringing a similar motion to vary on three separate occasions,
resulting in numerous adjournments of the defendants’ motion and several wasted
court appearances. This delayed the ultimate hearing of the defendants’ motion
from January to September 2007. As indicated earlier in this endorsement, the
bringing of the motions to vary, particularly the last one before me, was
improper and unnecessary and taken through negligence, mistake or excessive
caution. The motions to vary were ill founded and were repeated despite
indications by Brown J. and myself that the costs orders had not been appealed
and there were no grounds to vary. Both the defendants’ and the plaintiff’s
motions could have been, and should have been, dealt with in one or at the most
two attendances, rather than five.

[
32
]

The defendants’ Costs Outline indicates that the defendants have
incurred actual costs of $28,897 (inclusive of $26,706 in fees and $2,191 in
disbursements), which they claim on a partial indemnity basis in the amount of
$22,806. This includes the costs of their motion to dismiss or stay the action
and the plaintiff’s cross-motion before me to vary the prior costs orders. None
of these costs have yet been assessed. Both motions are significantly
intertwined and the defendants are entitled to the costs of both motions. The
Costs Outline specifically excludes the costs of the motion before Brown J. The
above totals do not include G.S.T. or the costs of making costs submissions.

[
33
]

Based on all of the above, it is easy to understand the time put in
on these motions of 29.5 hours by Mr. Mazzuca (counsel with carriage of the action),
89.6 hours by Ms. Kotsopoulos (who was counsel on the motion at each
attendance) and 16.6 hours by a law clerk and student. The hourly rate on a
partial indemnity scale claimed for Mr. Mazzuca (a 1993 call) ranging between
$221.25 and $225 and for Ms. Kotsopoulos (a 2003 call) ranging between $123.75
and $146.25 is not only fair and reasonable, but is at the lower end of the
appropriate range. The disbursements claimed are reasonable. Although the
principle of indemnity, including rates charged and hours spent is a factor set
out in rule 57.01(1)(0.a), the fixing of costs is more than an arithmetic
exercise of multiplying hours by hourly rates. The award must be fair and
reasonable in the circumstances. Although the time spent was dramatically increased
because of the multiple motions and attendances caused by the plaintiff, the
amount fixed must be reduced somewhat to account for the fact that the issues
were similar (albeit with differences) at each attendance, and that some
duplication is likely to have been incurred because of the involvement of both
Mr. Mazzuca and Ms. Kotsopoulos. I have also considered the partial success of
the plaintiff on the motion, albeit granted with the court’s indulgence, and
have taken into account the plaintiff’s financial circumstances.

[
34
]

In my view fair and reasonable costs of these motions in all the
circumstances, inclusive of disbursements and G.S.T. is the sum of $12,000.
This sum will be divided as between Mr. Guiste and the plaintiff, with the
plaintiff’s portion payable in instalments as outlined in these reasons. Given
the multiple motions and attendances and the prior awards of costs, the
plaintiff would reasonably have been aware of the mounting costs and the total would
not be beyond the reasonable expectations of herself or Mr. Guiste.

ORDER

[
35
]

The costs of the defendants’ motion to dismiss or stay the action
and the plaintiff’s motion to vary shall be to the defendants fixed in the sum
of $12,000.00 and payable as follows:

(a)

The sum of $4,000 shall be paid personally by Ernest Guiste,
solicitor for the plaintiff, within 30 days of the date this costs endorsement
is released.

(b)

The sum of $8,000 shall be paid by the plaintiff at the rate of $50
per month on the first day of each and every month commencing with the first
month following the month in which the stay of this action is lifted, with any
outstanding balance payable upon final disposition of the action in any event
of the cause.

___________________________

Master R. Dash

DATE:

December 4, 2007

[1]
A costs award against Mr. Guiste personally was not considered on
that motion since the defendants had not put him on notice under rule 57.07(2),
as they have now done on the current motion.

[2]
The costs of the first motion to vary, which was before me and was withdrawn
and the third motion to vary, which was before me and dismissed are included as
costs considered herein. The costs of the second motion to vary, which was
heard by Brown J., is not included as they were the subject of an award of
costs by Brown J.

[3]

Courts of Justice Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, section 133(1)

[4]

Burrell v. Peel Police Services
,
[2007] O.J. No. 1638
. The
motion was heard April 27 and the decision released April 30, 2007.

[5]

Walsh v. 1124660
Ontario
Limited
,
2007 CanLII 4789 (ON SC)
, [2007] O.J. No. 639 (S.C.J.).
This was referred to in my reasons on the motion for a stay herein as Walsh #1,
and I continue that designation in these reasons. A subsequent costs decision,
referred to as Walsh #2 dealt with whether costs should be payable by the
plaintiff personally.

[6]

Young v. Young
,
1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3

[7]

Walsh
#1
, at para.
7, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22

[8]

Walsh
#1
at para.
7, 13, 14, 23

[9]

Walsh
#1
at para.
25

[10]
Now reported as
Burrell v. Peel Police Services
,
[2007] O.J.
No. 4232

[11]

Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian Jew Outreach
,
[2007]
O.J. No. 2140 at para. 69
.

[12]
